"Al" McGall gives them a hard workout from 4:30 to 6:00, and is so ready to grin that it seems as though he has some promising material up his sleeve. An informal meet was held with N. Y. headline: TRACK REVIEW
transcription: The past track season, although not exeedingly brilliant, was very eventful. At the outset, due to the loss of Perry Roberts and Mesloh, the sport seemed tottering on its last legs. Both of these men could always be depended upon to score heavily for the Red and Gray. Fortunately, however, the incoming class proved equal to the task of filling up the ranks. The track team, while not running away with the meets, always made an honorable showing. The N. Y. U. meet was lost by a few points only. In the Rutgers and New England meets, Stevens stood comparatively high. But it was at Penn Relays that Stute men romped their way to a first place. There is no doubt that the Stute had a crackerjack running team, which if supported by field and weight men of equal calibre, would have cleaned up. This defficiency of field men has been a longstanding obstacle at Stevens. Al McGall was able, however, to develop some local talent to such a pitch, that several records were broken. In the Middle States meet "Len" Bloss broke the broad-jumping record. "Johnny" Bray broke the javelin record, and "Doug" Goodale the shot-put record. DeGarmo lowered the time for the half-mile by two seconds. In the Middle States meet, Woodward ran two miles in less time than the Stute record, but, not winning first place, his record is not official. As in all the other sports, the track team looks forward to an even brighter career next season.
summary: A season review noting Stevens' track team overcame early graduation losses to post an honorable season, highlighted by Bloss, Bray, Goodale, and DeGarmo breaking Stute records at the Middle States meet.

headline: TRACK SQUAD IN MIDDLE STATES — Stute Men Finished Fifth In Field Of Fourteen Colleges — BLOSS BREAKS RECORD IN BROAD JUMP
transcription: On Saturday, May 15th, the varsity track team competed against twelve eastern college track squads in the Middle States Track Meet, held at Rutgers. Twelve and a half points were scored by the Stute team which netted a fifth place in the meet. Bloss was the star of the afternoon when, with a 22½-foot broad jump, he established a new record for the Middle States meet. He also placed third in the hundred yard dash. Woodward took third place in the two mile run and Ellis third in the two-twenty yard dash. Goodale tied with Hood of Swarthmore for fourth place in the shot put. headline: N. Y. U. WINS DUAL TRACK MEET
transcription: On Wednesday, May 12th, in a meet in which the winner could not be picked until the last event had finished, N. Y. U. beat Stevens in track by the score of 61-51. It was extremely unfortunate that the Stute weight men and the jumpers were unable to do as well as the runners in the track meet with N. Y. U. last Wednesday. Of the eight running events, Stute men took 5 firsts, while out of the six remaining events we received only a single first. This meet was marked by the breaking of four Stute records. De Garmo ran the half mile in 2 min.-4 sec. dimishing the record by 1 sec. In the 1 mile run, Brown breasted the tape in 4 min. 44.1-5 sec. Bray's record-breaking throw of 149 ft. was insufficient to win the javelin throw. Goodale also broke the college record in the shot put. Brown, De Garmo, Bray, Woodward, and Bloss all found their way to firsts.

headline: PROGRESS NOTED IN INDOOR SPORTS TRACK
transcription: Have you noticed some fellows jogging around the track lately? Has it ever occurred to you that these men are not out for their health, but for business? No? Well, those fellows are our track team and are just trying to get started early. They are there to get their muscles loosened up and their condition developed and have been working for two weeks. Both the old and new material are showing up very well and should develop into a formidable squad. The team has been entered in several New York indoor games to give it experience and to put it in condition for the coming spring meets and the Penn Relays. Manager Meigs and Asst. Mer. Burritt have been working hard and have compiled a well balanced program, If the Stute gets behind the team, indications are that it will see some mighty good work in the spring.

headline: MITCHELL, TRACK TEAM COACH — Captain De Garmo Lost To Stevens' Runners
transcription: Manager Burritt announced Thursday that winter track practice is scheduled to begin on October 10. From then on daily workouts will be held. Graduation has broken up the team to a considerable extent, but the interclass meet last May brought out several underclassmen with ability in this line. The first business of the remaining varsity men was the election of a captain to succeed George De Garmo, who has withdrawn from the Stute. All those who wish to try out for Assistant Manager are also asked to report at the present time to L. D. Burritt, '22. In accordance with the policies of all teams, the underclassmen are urged to try out at once in order to build up for future varsity teams. Unlike other activities, track offers a diversity of positions for men with ability in various activities. Contrary to the usual opinions, track is not a sport for runners only but those who have muscle in other portions of their body are also useful. In brief, track is a sport for a man who wishes to work hard to get himself in condition and to keep himself physically perfect. The chief advantages of such training are the acquisition of excellent health and the opportunity of making personal records, Unlike other sports, the success of a track team depends upon individual, together with team work. Each man has, therefore a better opportunity to make a name for himself as an athlete. Coach Mitchell will have charge of the team during the winter season, since "Doc" Davis is coaching the basketball squad.
summary: Winter track practice begins under Coach Mitchell after Captain De Garmo withdrew from Stevens, and the team seeks underclassmen to rebuild.

headline: STUTE LOSES TRACK MEET TO DELAWARE
transcription: The Stevens track team came out on the short end of a 66—38 score in its match with Delaware here on Saturday, April 22, The wearers of the blue captured nine firsts, while the Stute took four. Dodge was easily the shining star for the Stute, garnering a total of 16 points and breaking the Stute record for the discus throw. He took firsts in the 120-yard high hurdles and discus throw and second in the shot put and high jump. Wiggins crossed the line first in the 880-yard run and boosted Steven's total by 5 points, Busch took another first by putting the shot the furthest. In the 100-yard dash, Fluri finished a close second to the Delaware man, who breasted the tape at 10.4/5 seconds. Three more points were added by Arlt, Everitt and Balch each. Arlt was second in the mile and Everitt in the two mile, while Balch made his three points in the pole vault. Delaware proved best in the distance runs, while Stevens made a fair showing in the field events. The time for all runs was comparatively slow, and, except for the discus throw of 106 feet by Dodge, no records were approached.

transcription: The track meet held here on last Saturday resulted in a win for Brooklyn Poly by the slim margin of 61½ to 46½. headline: FAIR SHOWING MADE — Stute Records For 220 and Discus Are Broken — DODGE'S HEAVY SCORING IS FEATURE OF SEASON
transcription: The recent interclass track meet completed the season for the Stevens' track team, and it has been a fairly successful year in many ways. Notwithstanding the fact that only one of the dual meets resulted in a victory for the Stute, it must be remembered that the defeats were not decisive by any means, as the team always gave their opponents a stiff fight and most of the meets lost were lost by a very slim margin. The season opened with the meet with Delaware here on April 22. Delaware has a fine squad and deserved the victory which they gained by the score of 66 to 38, Delaware's distance runners ran up her total considerably, while the work of Dodge and Busch in the field events was worthy of credit. Dodge was easily the Stute's individual star, running up a total of 21 points and breaking the Stute record in the discus event, with a throw of 109 feet. The C. C. N. Y. track men were encountered next on May 6, and the Stute scored an overwhelming victory to the tune of 89 to 28, The Stevens men were in fine fettle and captured every first place, with one exception; they captured the lead from the start and were never in danger. Dodge again scored heavily. A team composed of Mattimore, Martine, Herbell and Wiggins represented Stevens at the Penn Relays. They were entered in the Technical College class, which included such teams as Rensselaer, Georgia Tech, Brooklyn Poly and Worcester Tech. The competition was very strong, but Stevens managed to finish in fourth place. The Haverford meet was the next on the schedule and this took place away from home on May 11. Although the score, which favored Haverford by 76 to 50, does not indicate such, yet it was probably the best showing the Stute team made during the season. Both teams were in good form, the weather and track favored and all of the runs were made in very fast time. Haverford had some speedy men in the distance runs, but the feature was the running of Olsen for Stevens. He broke the Stute record in the 220 yd. dash by 2-5 seconds, finishing in 22 3-5 seconds and did the 100 yd. dash in 10 1-5 seconds. Dodge continued his point-getting in the field events. On the following Saturday, May 14, the representatives of Brooklyn Poly succeeded in nosing out Stevens by the score of 66 to 49, The meet was hard-fought and the last few events decided the meet. Most of the victor's points were scored through the efforts of two men, while Olsen, Martine, Busch, and Dodge helped to swell the Stute total, the latter again making a record-breaking throw of the discus. The interclass meet on May 18 served to show that there is fine material for next year's track team in the Frosh class, many of whom have tried out for the squad this year. They rolled up a total of 52 1-2 points, mainly due to the work of Fluri and Brown who will bear watching, The Juniors were a close second with 48 1-2 points, the Seniors were third and the Sophs trailed. The work of Dodge, the captain, stands out most prominently; he accounted for 79 points during the season and was always a reliable and consistent scorer. Olsen did some fine work in the dashes, Martine scored often in his events and Busch was always good for some points in the field events. With the Frosh material the coming season appears promising.
summary: A full season recap: Stevens' dual meets were mostly close losses (Delaware, Haverford, Brooklyn Poly) except a lopsided win over C.C.N.Y., with Dodge (79 points on the season) breaking Stute records in the discus and Olsen breaking the 220-yard dash record.

headline: FALL TRAINING FOR TRACK SQUAD NOW ON
transcription: Coach Mitchell called a meeting of the entire track squad on Monday, October 1, at 4:30, at the Gym. About twenty-five candidates, including many members of last year's squad were present. Coach Mitchell explained to the men that although Stevens does not participate in any meets until spring, he considered it best that the entire squad do some cross-country work in order to get into a semblance of good condition by that time. He explained that the purpose of cross-country work was not to produce a cross-country team, but to get the wind and legs of every man in the squad into shape. He explained that it is as important for a jumper to have his legs in condition as it is for a miler. He closed the meeting with instructions to each group of men as to how to pursue their training. Track practice is to be held three times per week, on Monday, Tuesday and Thursday. Although basketball and lacrosse are claiming quite a number of track men for the time being, it is expected that they will keep themselves in trim for that time when they will be free to follow the cinder path. Although a large number of men are now out for practice, Coach Mitchell is far from satisfied with the showing. There are a large number of men in the Freshman and Sophomore classes who might become good material and it is their duty to Stevens to report to practice as soon as possible.

headline: THE CINDER PATH.
transcription: Although track as an intercollegiate sport has been discontinued for two years at Stevens the persistent activity of the lovers of this sport brings it to the attention of the school once more. The Red and Gray has been represented in several of the open meets with quite satisfying results and it very possible that the coming spring will see the sport reinstated. In a busy college such as ours, track furnishes an exceptional opportunity for the students to gain athletic development because of the convenience in arranging practice. While a coach is needed to direct and control the men, it is not necessary for the entire team to practice together as in most sports. The individual men may keep in condition by practicing whenever they have free time, supplementing this with calisthenics at home. It is the drilling of the individuals to work as a unit that requires most of the time in team sports. For this reason track is the form of athletics which is least liable to disturb the ideal balance between curriculum and extra-curriculum work. The sport itself is probably second only to football in prominence in intercollegiate circles. It is also an outstanding form of international competition, the Olympic Games and the periodic invasion of the combined Oxford-Cambridge teams being evidences of its popularity. The sport is furthermore of such a nature that there is practically no danger of serious injury during practice or competition. It is a sport which is free from the taint of professionalism. Its following is from a high type of people and clean sportmanship is the rule. Athletic competition in moderation is recognized as being of great benefit to the participants. It is desirable that as many as possible be given the opportunity to derive the benefits of such competition. We have a cinder track and the necessary equipment for a track team. Is it fair that the men with ability in track be denied the proper outlet and a reasonable amount of incentive to develop themselves as long as conditions are such as to make it possible to provide them? headline: Student Opinion
transcription: To the Editor of the STUTE. The attention of the student body will soon turn to the spring sports. Last year the Stute was represented by teams in tennis, baseball and lacrosse, and there is a possibility that this year track will be reinstated as an intercollegiate sport. In a college of the size and type of Stevens there is danger that by having too many squads at work at the same time, each will interfere with the others in drawing material from the student body. How will the reinstatement of track affect the other spring sports? We understand that the men interested in the renewal of track activities are not members of any other spring sports team, so that this year no noticeable difference would be made in the make-up of these teams. But it is certain that in future years track must draw some men who would otherwise make good in baseball, tennis or lacrosse, especially the latter. The popularity of track is undoubtedly more widespread than that of lacrosse, but the latter is rapidly gaining nation-wide favor. At Stevens lacrosse was instituted as an intercollegiate sport in 1885 and track in 1910, The Institute is probably better known in connection with lacrosse than any with other sport. The track team of a small college cannot hope to compete creditably with the teams of larger institutions, while in lacrosse we meet teams representing the greatest colleges and universities in the East. In a former issue of the STUTE mention was made of the periodic invasion of the Oxford-Cambridge track team. We have never been in a position to meet this team on the cinder path, but we have played the Oxford-Cambridge lacrosse team and expect to meet them again in the coming season. Also in track where everything depends on the individual, natural ability is of paramount importance. In lacrosse it is easier to develop players because the responsibility rests upon the team and not upon the individual. In a recent survey of technical colleges conducted by Director John A. Davis, of our Physical Education Department, it was found that less men with native athletic ability and preparatory school training in athletics come to Stevens than to any of the other institutions in our class. From the student standpoint there should be a team for those interested in track if they find pleasure in participation in that sport. However, pleasure in sport comes from striving and making a commendable showing, not necessarily brilliant. To do this a well balanced team is necessary, but even with a student body twice the size of the present one, it was found difficult to round out a track team to compete successfully with teams of other colleges. (Signed) K. FINSTERBUSCH, '26.

headline: CROSS COUNTRY MEET TAKEN BY SOPHOMORES
transcription: Last Saturday the sophomores won the first interclass cross country run in the history of Stevens. By scoring first and fourth places and having their three remaining men finish well up they came off with the good score of 38. The freshmen were close on their heels with a 43, the first freshman coming in fifth. The juniors were third with 55. President Davis fired the starting gun that sent nineteen men off on the long grind of two and a half miles, which seventeen finished. As the pack rounded the gym and started up the hill below the Castle, Peters '31, took the lead. He was running easily and was never headed. Cockerill, '30, who was expected to win was running poorly. He did not seem able to get going, and after the first mile and a half began to fall back. Hendricks '29, was running behind Peters. The rest of the pack straggled along 150 or 200 yards behind. Peters rounded the chem. lab. and started for the finish line on the track with Hendricks at his heels. Hendricks here made a great bid for first place putting everything he had into a final dash to pass Peters. The sophomore, however, had just enough reserve to uncork a last sprint, and he led the way home by a matter of inches. The first five to finish were, Peters, '31, Hendricks, '29, Cockerill, '30, Mount, '31, Vidosi, '32. The interclass cross country run last Saturday proved pretty interesting, The finish was a neck and neck race between Peters, '31 and Hendricks, '29, Peters winning because he had the longest nose. Cockerill, '30, who was favored to win, had a bit of trouble and finished a poor third. Fourteen others straggled in from time to time and there were several tight battles for places. The winning time was 16:20 which is not at all bad for two and a half miles. Cross country running looks as if it had come to stay. Give the boys a big hand!

headline: RUTGERS WINS CROSS COUNTRY RUN IN DARK
transcription: Rutgers won the cross-country run against Stevens held last week, winning the first five places. The major part of the run was held in the dark and a complete result of the finishes is not available, Peters, of the Stevens team, was running up with the leaders until he tripped and fell over some obstruction. transcription: There is now some interest in track and field sports around the campus. Apparently some of the boys have found out that there are more kinds of tracks than the ones that trains move on. A group of freshmen who have done some running in prep schools are behind the movement to organize an informal or unofficial track team which will be able to compete in dual meets with other schools. There is an attempt being made to arrange an interclass track meet, in the hopes of discovering someone who can move his legs just a bit faster than the next fellow. There hasn't been an interclass meet in three years, and as we recall they used to provide a lot of fun and exercise for some of the boys who otherwise did nothing. There must be a few men at the Stute who can run or jump, and if three men can be found for each event the challenge of the Savage School can be accepted. Track faded from the list of Varsity sports some years back, when it was felt that there were not sufficient men to maintain a track team in the same season with lacrosse. It is quite true that good track men usually make good lacrosse players, and as lacrosse is probably the oldest and most representative spring sport at Stevens it is only fair that it should remain. However if some of the boys do a little running before the lacrosse season starts, no one can complain. It all helps to put them in condition. A team has been entered in the freshman medley relay of the Manhattan College Games. This relay consists of four legs of 220, 440, 600, and 880 yards. It takes quite a versatile bunch to form such a group, and if these freshmen can even come close to winning they will form a dandy nucleus for a prospective track team.

transcription: Talking about track and field athletics, which nobody ain't, the present interclass track meet has aroused considerable interest in the ancient Olympic pastimes. It seems that there are a number of the boys who could make a creditable showing in dual meets if they trained seriously. There is some talk of entering a team in the coming Penn Relays. There are four or five half-decent quarter milers around the Stute, who could do fairly well. Last Saturday, on a muddy track and a brisk wind blowing across the field, the winning time was something like 54 flat. There is no great strength in the field events, though one or two of the boys did heave the weights and the javelin right smartly. With a little coaching, some hard work and plenty of enthusiasm it might be possible to hold a few meets with some of the near-by colleges. Of course the whole business is more or less unofficial, and anyone taking part in these nebulous meets would get nothing but the fun out of it, Still, it might create so much interest that—Oh, well, look at soccer.

headline: Track Men to Meet For Reorganization
transcription: The track team will hold a reorganization session this afternoon at 12:30 in the lacrosse room of the gymnasium. Edward Castro, '33, has issued a call for all candidates, especially for the underclassmen. Any freshman who has run in high or prep school should continue to run under Stute colors. The team has received challenges from Cooper Union, Savage, Newark College of Engineering, and Long Island University for dual track meets. The University of Pennsylvania has invited the track team to participate in its annual track and field carnival to be held at Franklin Field April 24 and 25. Last year the harriers defeated Savage, 63 to 36, but were nosed out by Cooper Union, 41 to 40. The nucleus of the team is composed of Castro, Nefzger, Mount, Naughton, Ciulla, Garroway, and Alton. As most of the track meets are held on our field, the student body will have several opportunities to watch the team in action. In view of last year's season, it is felt that a team could be reorganized to meet intercollegiate competition. It is essential for the continued success of the team that new material be obtained, and it is therefore urged upon all who are interested to come to today's meeting. A special need is felt for those who have any ability in putting the shot, in high jumping, or in pole-vaulting. Experience is no requisite, and instruction will be given. Everyone will be on an equal basis and will have the same chance to make the team. Track requires less practice than other sports at Stevens, two hours a week being sufficient for the average man.

headline: Twenty Candidates Out for Track Team
transcription: On Wednesday, March 4th, over twenty candidates answered the call for the reorganization of the track team. This turnout decided the question as to whether a team should be formed or not, and, consequently, the invitation for the Penn Relays was accepted. The squad will send four men to this meet, each to run a quarter-mile leg. At the meeting more than eight men registered to run the quarter-mile, which means that of this group the fastest quartet will pound the track at Philadelphia, on April 24 and 25. Following the Penn Relays, the team will meet Savage, Cooper Union, and Newark College of Engineering on successive Saturdays. The dual meets with Long Island University and Brooklyn City College are pending but, in all probability, will be held in the early part of June. Other than these dual meets, the team will compete in various club meets and A. A. U. games. As for material, the team has a good number of sprinters, middle distance men and broad jumpers. The field section of the group is quite weak, however, lacking pole vaulters, shot putters, discus throwers, and high jumpers. For indoor practice the men are forced to practice on the balcony track in the gym or at nearby armories, until the weather permits for outdoor competition, Another serious handicap is the lack of a coach or faculty advisor to help the team. Last year, Mr. Gingrich rendered invaluable services towards the formation of a team. His absence has left the squad without the guidance of a coach. Plans are being made for holding an interclass track meet, the exact date of which will be made public in the near future. Last year the class of 1931 won the meet by a close margin. In these meets there is a possibility of discovering a star who is not aware of his talent.

transcription: Speaking of the track team, it would be interesting to learn just what this group hopes to accomplish. Each year the team reorganizes, and a small group of men practice, until summer, when with the closing of college they go their way and nothing is done until next spring, when the process is duplicated. The entire effort seems utterly useless, since those men who comprise the group realize and admit the fact that, first, they have not enough men, regardless of quality to form a regular track team; second, that the few men who are available are far from being exceptionally good, and third, that a well equipped track team requires standards and hurdles and that these are rather expensive and cannot be afforded by the group, or by the athletic association. We are very much in favor of a variety of sports at Stevens, but we do not feel that an organized track team can justify itself. However, we heartily approve Director Davis' plan of, first, encouraging sports at Stevens, which are useful, as a means of recreation, in later life; and, second, increasing the number of simple sports so that every man will find at least one sport in which he is interested and fairly proficient.

headline: January Indicator Has Prize Article
transcription: Dear Mr. Editor: It is with keen interest that, from time to time, I read the headings of your news items and occasionally digest the descriptive matter in your columns, thereby, in a general way, keeping informed as to what is transpiring at the Old Stone Mill. It was with particular interest that I noticed in your March 18th issue that some enthusiastic reporter, possibly more than casually interested in lacrosse, was waiting with a lead pipe for the track team to come up for the third time so as to help it go down never to return. It is regrettable that track has no similar representative to give it the publicity it deserves. While it is true that a fully equipped track team requires standards, hurdles, shot, discus and a vaulting pole, some of which equipment lasts indefinitely, it is my recollection that the wood-shop could quite satisfactorily handle the construction of the hurdles for the cost of the raw material. While it is granted that neither Stevens nor any of the other smaller colleges will be likely to develop a track squad which can interest U. of P., Yale, Princeton, etc., it is enlightening news that the quality of our present athletic material is so inferior to that of ten or fifteen years ago that it is impossible to put a team in the field. This is especially enlightening in view of the number of track records which have been broken in open competition during the past year. Practically no high school has a lacrosse team and it is, therefore, necessary in four years to coach and develop raw material into a seasoned team, without having the benefit of high school training as is possible with the track candidates. So far at the Stute, lacrosse has been successful in diverting just enough men from track, especially in the distance events, to result in a mediocre instead of first rate small college team. [unclear] The point has been made that track does not pay for itself. This will also apply to all the other spring sports and it should be remembered that a balanced track team does not necessarily require two different men for each event. The writer remembers when the Eastern Intercollegiate Championships were nearly won one year at Springfield by two men and when, not so long ago, teams from N. Y. U., C. C. N. Y., and Rutgers tasted defeat from the wearers of the red and gray. As your track reporter is sadly conspicuous by his absence, it would be appreciated if you could find space to include the above in your sporting columns. Yours for track, A. PERRY ROBERTS, Captain 1919.

headline: The Field Day
transcription: Editor-in-Chief, THE STUTE. Dear Sir: I would like to call to the attention of the student body and the Physical Education Department, an old Stevens institution, Field Day, which has long passed into oblivion. It is time that steps were taken to revive this gala day, as a means of bolstering up the fast-disappearing school spirit. Competition would be between classes, and should command an excellent response. Back in the old days there was enough interest in this type of sport to support a track team that was really good. It has been said that Stevens is too small a school to support a track team. Nevertheless, present enrollment far surpasses that during the years 1905-1915, when the track team had some of its most successful [seasons]. A stepping stone to the [return] of the track team would be the annual field day. It would require a large number of entrants, what with eliminations, semi-finals, etc. and that is what we most desire. The complete roster of field [events should include] those which are adapted to a large number of entrants. Prizes should not be considered, as they would entail a large expense. Certificates of merit should serve the purpose, as the entries are to be encouraged, not on a basis of prizes to be won, but for the fun, sport, and benefits to be derived from the active participation in the events. Banner awards could be made to the winning class. As a starter, to give the students something to consider, I will list the old-time Stevens track records, as given by the Link of 1923: 100-yard dash 10 sec. 220-yard dash 22 3-5 sec. 440-yard dash 51 2-5 sec. 880-yard run 2 min. 2 4-5 sec. One mile 4 min. 43 3-5 sec. Broad jump 22 ft. 6 in. High jump 5 ft. 10¾ in. Shot put [39] ft. 9 in. Javelin throw [149] ft. Discus throw [110] ft. Hammer throw [97] ft. 10 in. Pole vault 10 ft. 2 in. With these marks to shoot at, an interclass field day should reveal just how many potential track men we have in the school.

headline: Field Day
transcription: TRACK AND FIELD returned to Castle Point last Friday, and from the enthusiasm accorded the events, similar meets should be continued in the future. Track as a sport is not an innovation at the Stone Mill; for years the Institute boasted a varsity track squad, and inter-class meets were staged until the late '20's when they were discontinued because of waning support by the students. Varsity track was abolished about 1924. Stevens also had a Field Day, the date on which the interclass meets were staged. Results were carefully handed down from year to year, and the college track records stood as a challenge to participants. Old accounts from about 1918 disclose that Red and Gray track feats are the "100-10 secs;" "220-23 secs;" Running Broad Jump-21 ft., 9½ in. These results are quite commendable when one considers that recognized world records in those years differed very slightly. Rutgers and Stevens had their own special track rivalry and some of the records still unmatched by present day Scarlet trackmen were established during these dual meets. In the fall of 1928, cross-country running was introduced, and a course of about three and one-half miles was laid out on the grounds. It had the "distinction of being the only course in the world within twenty minutes of Wall Street." Informal meets were held with the New York Stock Exchange and Rutgers. But, as numerous activities here, it finally gave up the ghost because of non-support. However, judging from the standpoint of keen participation and interest displayed, another track meet is something that the A. A. Council should be concerned with. If the A. A. should decide to sponsor inter-class meets, it certainly would further college spirit, and the awarding of class numerals to the victors would provide more incentive.

headline: Cross-Country
transcription: A PROPOSAL will be submitted to the A. A. Council this Friday, and provided the Council accepts, a cross-country squad will return to Castle Point. The action arises from numerous student inquiries about the possibility of the formation of such a squad, and Mr. O'Keefe, on their behalf, has formally asked the Council for its sanction as he contemplates assuming the position of coach. Judging from student interest shown and acknowledging Chief O'Keefe's capacities as a mentor, we can safely predict a team worthy of representing the Red and Gray. In former years, the Stone Mill had both track and cross-country squads, which eventually died because of waning student support. Poor support of these sports has been attributed to the fact that promising aspirants preferred team athletics such as lacrosse, baseball or tennis rather than individual performance. The route of the old cross-country course on the campus will be followed, and while perhaps not adequate, it will serve as a conditioner for the real tests which will come next term. Inter-collegiate competition will be furnished by colleges in the Metropolitan area, and the course used will probably be the one in Van Cortlandt Park in the Bronx, which has been the scene of similar college and prep school meets. When inclement weather forces the squad indoors, the oval track in the gym will be utilized, and Mr. O'Keefe's ultimate goal is the entering of the squad in Madison Square Garden meets during the winter season.

headline: Richard Meidell to Enter Penn Relay
meet_or_event: 53rd Annual Invitational Pennsylvania Relay Carnival (Penn Relays)
transcription: Richard Meidell, '50, will represent Stevens in the 53rd Annual Invitational Pennsylvania Relay Carnival, which will be held at the University of Pennsylvania on April 25 and 26. This meet consists mainly of relays of various types, including the Sprint Medley, Two Mile Relay, and Shuttle Hurdle Relay. Field events are included as well as the hundred yard dash, and the 120 high hurdles. Dick will compete in the broad jump event, against such schools as Illinois, which currently holds the National Championship, Michigan, Army, Navy, Dartmouth, Ohio State, and Michigan State. Dick is an all around athlete, having earned varsity letters in football, baseball, and track while in Redford High School in Detroit. In addition, he played first base on the Great Lakes nine while he was in the Navy, and upon discharge, entered the University of Detroit, where he was a member of the football squad. He is a member of the A.A.U., and of the New York Athletic Club Track Team, which at present holds the team title in the National A.A.U. As far as his expectations for the meet go, Dick says that he jumped 28 feet at Great Lakes last year, and believes he can do it again at the Penn Relays.

headline: Track Club Discussed in Letter
transcription: Editor, THE STUTE Dear Sir: A small band of running enthusiasts here at Stevens are bound together in a very loosely knit group called the Stevens Track Club. As clubs go, this is not a true club for there are no dues, no organizational meetings, and up to now, no activity. These men are known as members of the Stevens Track Club only by their willingness to pound themselves dizzy on the treadmill in the Walker Gymnasium, often called a race track. More and more of them may be observed as the indoor season nears and now their leaders wish to announce that there will be time trials for the 220, 440, 880 yards and the mile run. These trials were held Saturday afternoon, January 10, 1948. The best times will qualify for positions on one or more relay teams for intercollegiate competition. We also wish to announce the fact that Coach Tom Triol has offered to pilot these relay teams through the indoor season. Coach Triol is an experienced trackman and an ex-champion at his specialty, the high hurdles. With such help we stand a good chance to give a heretofore neglected sport at Stevens a fine start. Later in the spring, the Track Club plans to develop into a healthy squad including all running events except hurdling (due to lack of hurdles), high and broad jumping, and all field events such as shot putting, discus throwing and perhaps javelin throwing. The lack of spacious practice fields and equipment curtails some of the track and field events we would like to see furthered. It is also planned to run intramural relays during the spring with a run off for the school championship on Spring Sports Day, as was done on a small scale last year. These plans will be presented to the Student Body as they fall due. John Shaw, 3F
summary: A letter announces the informal Stevens Track Club, with time trials held and Coach Tom Triol offering to guide relay teams through the indoor season, plus plans for a spring squad limited by lack of equipment.

headline: Just Rambling Around
transcription: The student body owes a vote of thanks to Walt Haass, who during the past year as commissioner of interclass sports, has done a tremendous job in making interclass sports an important activity at Stevens. We are looking toward Dick Bruneau, newly appointed commissioner, to build up interclass sports still further. In an effort to get more men active in interclass sports, Bruneau has interclass swimming and interclass track events on tap for next year. This is a major step in the right direction and could very well lead to the development of a Stute varsity swim team and the re-establishment of a varsity track team.

headline: Attention, Speedsters!!!
transcription: It has come to the attention of the writers of this column that the students are showing a supreme lack of interest in the Interclass Track Meet which is to be held on Wednesday, April 29. In an exclusive interview with Coach Frank Misar, we learned that this is the first meet of its kind at Stevens and that the gym department is hoping for a large turnout. However, Coach Misar said that the success of the event was solely in the hands of the student body which was at present lying down on the job. Come on, you guys, get off the seat of your pants and sign up for this student track meet. The rules are simply this: any student not on the Varsity or J.V. Baseball, Lacrosse or Tennis teams is eligible. Each man may enter any two of the following events: 100, 200, 440, and 600 yard dash, mile relay, high jump, and shot put. So, let's get on the ball, men. Contact your A.A. representative or sign up with Harold Shuster or Hank Bried via the mail rack or in person.

headline: SOPHOMORES COP INTERCLASS TRACK MEET—TUMSER STARS
transcription: The class of '55 took first place in Stevens initial interclass track meet Wednesday afternoon with a grand total of 25 points. The Junior's 21 points brought them second honors while the individual stars of the meet were Roy Tumser and Herb Graffweg. In the first event Tumser's 10.2 seconds in the 100 yard dash copped first place easily for the Sophs. Graffweg then retaliated for the juniors and in 58.4 seconds won the 440 yard dash. The sophomores took three out of four places in tossing the 12 pound shot, led again by Tumser with a hefty fling of 41 feet 8½ inches. Tumser racked up his third first by running the 220 in 23.3 seconds. The final event was the 880 relay which the Juniors, running Quitzau, Gatti, Kalika and Graffweg, consecutively, won with a time of 1 minute 45.6 seconds. The last event of the meet was the high jump which Red Graffweg, former N. Y. state secondary school high jump champ won with a tremendous leap of 6 feet 1 inch. A four man tie at over a foot below Graffweg's mark finished the meet. The Seniors came in third with 11½ points and the Frosh last with 8½. Roy Tumser breasts the tape two yards in front of Jerry Fischer to take the 220 in the interclass track meet.

headline: Rigid Training Is Expected
transcription: Prexy Jesse James of the Snoot revealed today that for the first time in its history, this glorious institution may actually have a track team. Said Jesse when accosted at the 'Box, "the boys who pole vaulted in high school have been complaining that their poles are losing rigidity through lack of use here." The president went on to explain that until now the boys have had to work out with their poles individually but that the sport is long since dead. It was obvious that a healthy solution had to be worked out. "Since my announcement early this morning," continued Jesse, "I've noticed that the boys are scrubbing their equipment fondly in anticipation of events to come." A tour of the campus by an enterprising Snoot reporter revealed that extensive preparations are being made for the coming [track] season. F. Q. Loin revealed that a thousand gross of Ex-Lax has been ordered to keep the milers running. In addition, material is being imported from local sources to keep the broad jumpers happy. Also, a special outhouse is being constructed for those who excel in putting the shot, Completion of these preparations is scheduled for early next month. In affiliation with these plans, the Gym Department has stated its desire to sponsor a swimming meet at the same time.

transcription: Interclass—The interclass sports season just past was marked by numerous forfeitures (reflecting the lack of class and school spirit so prevalent around the Stute) and inefficient scheduling by those in charge. A prime example was the IC track meet which was recently run off. It is hard to believe that the only publicity for this meet came through word of mouth, leaving the junior and senior classes with a decided lack of runners. Until race time, no schedule of events had been released, leading the managers to enter men in fictitious events. It is the hope of the sports department that these deficiencies will be rectified in the future.

transcription: To the Editor of the Stute: I'd like to call attention to a situation which is quite important, I think, to a number of people. Today (Wednesday) the freshmen won the interclass track meet, apparently by a comfortable margin. However, the Athletic Association did not announce the date of the track meet in the STUTE or any place else at any time. Thus, the arrangements for the meet were apparently left to the A.A. representatives and the junior class effort was a sign-up list, not making any notice of date or arrangements, put up a few days ago. As a result, a number of juniors, myself included, did not participate in the meet today although we carried the brunt of participation in the last two years. Incidentally, a mention was made over the Stevens Radio Network on Monday evening that the meet was scheduled for Saturday. What I hope this letter will do is to get a little more efficient action out of our Athletic Association. Word of mouth is not always the best or fairest method of communication. The fact that half of the school commutes shows the importance of more efficient publicity for better interclass support, something that's always being cried for in the STUTE. Stu Asselin '58

transcription: With the running of Saturday's track meet, which resulted in a sophomore triumph, interclass competition came to an end for another year. headline: CROSS-COUNTRY TO BE INTRODUCED AT STEVENS
transcription:
A short meeting was held last Wednesday at the gym of all those interested in the formation of a cross-country team. Professor Gingrich of the Language Department has had some experience in this sport, and he will act as mentor for the team.

Practice will be held Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays, with Professor Gingrich in charge. If sufficient interest is shown by the student body, this innovation may lead to the establishment of track as a regular varsity sport.

headline: CROSS COUNTRY TEAM HAS FINE FUTURE
transcription: Depending on the enthusiasm shown by students at Stevens, cross country running may be added to the list of sports in which we are represented on athletic fields. According to the coach of the team, Professor Gingrich, the plan at present is to make cross country an inter-class sport, in which class numerals may be won. Under this plan, each class would be represented by their best seven cross country runners. Already candidates for these teams are practising on Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday afternoons. [...] Professor Gingrich would consider twenty candidates from each class, a very encouraging start. As to future plans, it has been decided that if the calibre of the men chosen for the interclass teams is on a par with those of other colleges, it will be arranged for Stevens to have a team entered in some inter-collegiate contests, [and] at this time, cross country would be considered a major sport and accordingly varsity letters would be awarded to the members of the team. It is not too late to go out for the cross country team.
summary: A follow-up on the new interclass cross country program: Gingrich is targeting 20 candidates per class, with a path to varsity status and letters if the program proves itself against other colleges.

headline: CROSS COUNTRY RUN FOR HIGH SCHOOLS NOV. 24th
transcription:
Event Open to Public Schools of North Jersey to Be Run On Stevens Course

At a special meeting of the Student Council held last Thursday afternoon in President Davis' office, it was decided to hold an Interscholastic Cross Country Run, here at Stevens, on Saturday, November 24th. [...] The suggestion for the run came from President Davis, who proposed the matter to the Council for its consideration, and suggested that the Council be responsible for the necessary arrangements. Mr. Ginrich of the Department of Modern Languages, who has been coaching the candidates for interclass cross country, was also present at the meeting, and furnished several good suggestions as to the management of the affair. The course, which is two and one-half miles long, was planned by Dr. Davis and Mr. Ginrich.

After the Student Council had assumed control of the meet, there was considerable discussion of the various details connected with such an event. As a result of the discussion it was decided to limit the event to the Public High Schools of Northern New Jersey. Each school may enter a team consisting of seven men with three alternates. A cup will be awarded to the winning team, and as it is intended that the event shall be an annual one, the school winning the cup for three years will hold it permanently.

headline: Navy V-12 Physical Specialist at Stevens
transcription:
Chief Specialist Robert T. O'Keefe, well known sporting field figure in New Rochelle, and other Sound Shore areas, is now Director of the Cross Country and Indoor Track Teams, under the Navy's V-12 Program, as well as the baseball team. This latter team had a most successful season, beating Columbia 6 to 0.

Upon graduation from Chief Specialist School, Norfolk, O'Keefe was assigned to Norfolk Training Station as a member of the Physical Training School, where he took part as a Platoon Commander in the Destroyer Escort School. Later he was transferred to the Armed Guard School, where he put out six gun crews a week.

He also umpired the Norfolk Training and Air Stations baseball teams. The Norfolk Teams were practically all major league, if not Double A ball players, and they opposed such teams as the Washington Senators, Baltimore Orioles, North Carolina, Pre Flight Baseball Club, Richmond, Norfolk and Portsmouth of the Piedmont League.—New Rochelle Std.-Star.
